title: After 10 years, Columbus mother waits for closure in sons' deaths - NewsBreak
text:
By Isabel Cleary ,
6 hours ago
COLUMBUS, Ohio ( WCMH ) -- A Columbus mother has fought for justice for her sons since they were killed in Columbus in 2017. Now, with a new trial date approaching, she said delays are keeping her from finally being able to mourn.
The prosecutor’s office said it's ready for this trial; the defense attorney won’t answer calls or texts from NBC4. The victims’ mother, Tysha Hill said she needs the case to go to trial so, after almost 10 years, she can finally mourn.
“Energy never dissipates; it only transforms. I have become the air you breathe,” Hill reads. That's the phrase that keeps Hill going and greets loved ones as they visit Je’Ronn and Je'Vohn’s grave.

In March 2017, the brothers were found shot to death in their home.
“My world was ended. My life ended that day. My boys were gone,” Hill said.
Hill said she gave police a name that night: Brian Banks.
“He was not a stranger. he was someone who grew up running in and out of my house, running in and out of my mother's house, and that he had been living with my sons,” Hill said.
Seven years after their deaths, Banks was arrested and charged with the murders of the Hill boys. The case has not yet gone to trial.
NBC4 Investigates found the case has been continued more than 10 times. Each time, Hill has been in court.
“The case is about Je’Vohn and Je'Ronn Hill, and my presence there is to remind them of that,” Hill said. “At some point, I am going to hear the judgment from the jury. If it's not guilty, OK, I did what I was supposed to do. If it is guilty, great. I did what I was supposed to do.”
Appeals court to rule on EdChoice program’s constitutionality Three times the trial has been continued because the suspect refused to be transported.
“Sometimes when people refuse, it's hard to tell,” Capital University Associate Professor of Law Robert Barnhart said. “Sometimes somebody might be sick and it will be written as a refusal, so that's a little bit more on the unusual side if you have somebody multiple times refusing to come to court.”
Barnhart said the most recent continuances show the case is moving closer to trial.
“There's just so many things that can get in the way,” Barnhard said. “It’s not unusual to see multiple continuances that say, ‘Set for trial’. It's just kind of an indication that's where we are.”
Last December, the case was set for trial in April.
“After that, they set the next trial date for Oct. 19, but now, as that date approaches, the defense attorney is not communicating with the prosecutor's office,” Hill said.
NBC4 Investigates reached out to the defense attorney multiple times over two weeks: calling and texting, even stopping by his office. He never responded. Now, the case is being continued again.

Barnhart said preparing for these types of cases can be very difficult and there really is no average time it takes to go to trial.
